items.scenario: You ask Claude Code to 'add rate limiting to the public API' in a client repo you have never opened. Twenty minutes later it has edited eleven files and added a new middleware library; the team already had a rate-limit helper in lib/http.
items.question: What change to your workflow would most likely have prevented this?
options: Explore the code and agree a plan before allowing any edits
Switch to a more capable model so it finds existing helpers itself
Add 'be careful' and 'reuse code' to the end of the prompt
Accept the edits, then ask Claude to refactor onto the helper
items.explanation: Skipping the plan lets Claude commit to the first plausible approach across many files. A plan review is the cheapest point to inject knowledge it lacks (the existing helper) and to reject a new dependency.
distractors: A stronger model still guesses the approach without the plan step; the cost was the unreviewed direction, not capability.
Vague exhortations add no specific knowledge and leave the approach unreviewed.
Refactoring a coherent wrong design costs far more than correcting a plan, and the dependency still has to be unpicked.

items.scenario: Claude presents a plan in plan mode. Step 2 introduces a new ORM abstraction; your team's convention is to keep raw repositories.
items.question: What is the most effective response?
options: Approve it and fix step 2 during code review afterwards
Reject or edit step 2 with the reason, then approve the revised plan
Approve it, because plan mode guarantees nothing is changed
Exit plan mode and give the original request again in default mode instead
items.explanation: The plan is where your knowledge goes in. Editing or rejecting a step with a reason redirects the whole implementation before any file changes.
distractors: Fixing it after implementation means unwinding edits across files that all assumed the abstraction.
Approving the plan authorises implementation of that step; plan mode's no-edit property ends at approval.
Restarting in default mode throws away the exploration and removes the review point entirely.

items.scenario: A team's CLAUDE.md has grown to 400 lines: build commands, the current sprint goals, who is on call this week, and a narrative of last quarter's outages.
items.question: What should be done with it?
options: Keep it all; more context always improves Claude's answers on this codebase
Move it into auto memory so Claude manages it automatically
Keep commands, conventions and boundaries; move volatile content out
Split it into four CLAUDE.local.md files, one per developer
items.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads into every session, so every line costs context and stale weekly content misleads. It should hold stable instructions; history and rotas belong elsewhere.
distractors: Irrelevant and stale content dilutes the instructions that matter and costs tokens every session.
Auto memory is Claude's unreviewed, machine-local notes, not a place for team instructions.
Local files aren't shared, so the team loses the common instructions it needs.

items.scenario: Your ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md says 'always use yarn'; the project CLAUDE.md says 'use npm ci'. Claude uses yarn in some sessions and npm in others.
items.question: What is the best fix?
options: Rely on the project file overriding your personal file
Restate 'use npm' in every prompt for this project
Turn off auto memory so the instructions stop conflicting
Delete the yarn rule, or scope it so it can't apply here
items.explanation: CLAUDE.md files are concatenated into context, not merged by a rule engine, so contradictions aren't resolved deterministically (Claude may pick either). Resolve them in the files.
distractors: Load order makes the more specific file later, but both remain in context; the inconsistent behaviour shows recency is not a guarantee.
Per-prompt reminders add context and don't remove the standing contradiction.
Auto memory isn't the source of either instruction; disabling it doesn't touch the conflict.

items.scenario: A client NDA forbids unreviewed persistence of project details on engineers' machines. A developer notices Claude Code has been writing notes about the client repo between sessions.
items.question: What should the team do?
options: Turn auto memory off for the repo in settings, and record that in CLAUDE.md
Commit the auto memory file so the client's reviewers can audit what Claude noted
Delete the notes weekly but leave auto memory on
Use incognito mode in the claude.ai app instead
items.explanation: Auto memory is Claude's own machine-local notes, on by default. Where policy requires, turn it off with the documented setting (committed so it applies to everyone) and make the rule visible.
distractors: Committing unreviewed, self-contradicting notes spreads them further and doesn't satisfy a no-persistence rule.
Notes still persist between deletions, which is what the NDA forbids.
Incognito is a claude.ai app feature; it doesn't control Claude Code's local auto memory.

items.scenario: Three hours into a session, Claude starts re-introducing a bug it already fixed and forgets the agreed naming. /context shows the window mostly filled with old test output.
items.question: What is the best recovery?
options: Keep going and remind Claude of the naming convention every few turns
Raise effort to the maximum for the rest of the session
Write a handover note to a file, clear, and continue from the note
Run /compact with no instructions and carry on
items.explanation: The context is full of stale material. A deliberate handover in a file, then a fresh session, carries forward what matters and drops the noise.
distractors: Each reminder adds more context to an already overloaded window; the drift continues.
Effort doesn't free context; the problem is what's in the window.
An unsteered summary may drop exactly the decisions you need (naming, fixed bugs).

items.scenario: Claude ran a codemod script via Bash that rewrote 30 files. The result is wrong, so you rewind to the checkpoint before the prompt. Most files are still modified.
items.question: What explains this, and what is the safer habit?
options: Checkpoints expired; increase how many are kept
Rewind only works in plan mode; switch modes first
Bash-only file changes aren't snapshotted; commit before running scripts
The conversation was restored but not the code; rewind again and pick code only
items.explanation: Checkpoints track edits made through Claude's file tools. A Bash script's writes are opaque to the harness, so Git — committing before risky steps — is the real undo.
distractors: The checkpoint existed; the issue is what it covers, not retention.
Rewind isn't limited to plan mode.
Even a code restore can't bring back changes that were never snapshotted.

items.scenario: Claude reports 'all tests pass' after a refactor. You are about to approve and push.
items.question: What must you do before accepting the change?
options: Nothing more; passing tests prove the refactor is correct
Read every hunk of the diff, including changes to tests
Ask Claude to confirm it didn't break anything
Run the tests a second time to rule out flakiness
items.explanation: Never accept a diff unread. Tests passing is evidence, not proof — tests themselves may have been weakened, and unplanned changes can hide in a large diff.
distractors: Green tests can come from edited or deleted assertions.
Claude's self-report isn't independent verification.
A second run checks flakiness, not whether the change or the tests are right.

items.scenario: One teammate has set effort to max for everything, including bulk renames, and complains about slow, costly sessions. Another runs low effort while chasing an intermittent race condition and keeps getting shallow guesses.
items.question: What guidance should you give the team?
options: Match effort to the task: raise it for the race, lower it for renames
Standardise everyone on max so results are consistent across the team
Standardise everyone on low and rely on plan mode for the hard thinking
Leave effort alone and switch to a larger model for difficult bugs
items.explanation: Effort trades tokens and latency for reasoning depth. Mechanical edits gain nothing from it; hard debugging and design do. Set it per task rather than as a team-wide constant.
distractors: Max on mechanical work is slow and expensive with no quality gain; consistency of setting isn't consistency of results.
Plan mode structures the work but doesn't supply the reasoning depth a hard race-condition hunt needs.
Model choice and effort are separate levers; leaving effort at low still starves the hard task of reasoning.

items.scenario: In a monorepo, billing has strict money-handling rules that are irrelevant to the other 30 packages. Putting them in the root CLAUDE.md bloats every session.
items.question: Where should those rules live?
options: In the root CLAUDE.md, under a clear 'Billing only' heading
In each developer's personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
In a nested billing/CLAUDE.md or a path-scoped rule
In auto memory, which loads only when billing is touched
items.explanation: Nested directory CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules load only when Claude works on matching files, keeping the context small elsewhere while the rules are committed and reviewed.
distractors: A heading doesn't stop the root file loading in every session; the rules still cost context in all 30 other packages.
Personal files aren't shared, so teammates and CI never get the rules.
Auto memory isn't scoped by path and isn't a reviewed instruction source.
